cse-2014-3-cs-13.approach: Because a vertex is visited only if it is still unvisited, the chain of active recursive calls is always a simple path. So the maximum recursion depth equals the number of vertices on the longest simple path, and a suitable start vertex and neighbour order can always realise it.

steps.title: Depth = vertices on a simple path
steps.body: The active calls at any moment form a root-to-node path of the DFS tree, which is a simple path in the graph. Conversely, if DFS always tries the next vertex of a chosen simple path $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$ first, each $v_{i+1}$ is still unvisited when $v_i$ is processed, so depth $k$ is reached. Hence we need the longest simple path (counting vertices).

scene.caption: 21 vertices: two 3×3 grids joined through vertex 10

steps.title: Structure of the graph
steps.body: The only link between the two $3\times3$ grids is the cut vertex 10 on the bottom row. Vertex $p$ (above 10) and vertex 19 (right of the right grid) have degree 1, so they can only be endpoints of a path. A path that uses both grids goes left grid $\to 10 \to$ right grid, so it cannot contain $p$.

steps.title: Left grid: all 9 vertices
steps.body: Colour a $3\times3$ grid like a chessboard: 5 cells (corners + centre) of one colour, 4 edge-middles of the other. A path through all 9 cells must start and end on the 5-cell colour. The exit vertex 9 is a corner, so the snake $1\to2\to\dots\to9$ covers all 9 vertices and ends at the exit.

steps.title: Right grid: at most 9 more
steps.body: After 10 we enter the right grid at its bottom-left corner (11). Either the path covers all 9 right-grid vertices, or it ends at the middle-right vertex (18) and steps to the pendant 19. Vertex 18 is an edge-middle (other colour from the corner 11), so a path from 11 to 18 has an even number of vertices, at most 8; with 19 that is again 9. Either way the right side adds at most 9 vertices.

scene.caption: Path of 19 vertices; p and q unused

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $$9 + 1 + 9 = 19$$\nAny path starting at $p$ skips a whole grid and is shorter. Starting DFS at vertex 1 and following the path shown gives recursion depth **19**.

pitfalls: Answering 21 (the vertex count): both pendant vertices cannot lie on one simple path that crosses between the grids.
Ignoring the colour (parity) constraint inside each 3×3 grid.

steps.title: Recurrence
